sipnab reads the SIP and the audio that pass through Asterisk off the wire.
So it needs nothing from Asterisk: no module, no configuration change.

Asterisk is a [B2BUA](@/docs/glossary.md#b2bua). Every call through it is two SIP
calls, called legs:

- the caller's leg into Asterisk,
- Asterisk's leg out to the callee.

Each leg has its own Call-ID. sipnab does three things with the two legs:

- It lists them as two [dialogs](@/docs/glossary.md#dialog).
- It shows them together as one call flow.
- It measures the audio on each.

This guide adds sipnab to the Asterisk machine from
[Use Asterisk as your voice stack's PBX](@/docs/asterisk.md). It does the following:

- It watches a test call.
- It shows its two legs in the terminal interface.
- It explains it from a saved capture.
- It answers about it over MCP and the REST API.
- Finally, it receives Asterisk's own copies of its SIP over HEP.

**What works without Asterisk.** sipnab does not depend on Asterisk.

- The sections from "Watch a call through Asterisk"
  to "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST"
  use sipnab's own capture.
  - They work the same way beside any SIP server.
- The section "Receive Asterisk's HEP" is the one that uses an
  Asterisk module.
  - You can leave it out.

## Tested on

Every block on this page ran as written, in order, on 2026-10-12.

- It ran with sipnab 0.5.211 from its release package.
- It ran on the Debian 13 (kernel 6.12.63) and Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0)
  machines that [the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md) had set up.
- The terminal interface ran in a terminal 160 columns wide and 40 lines high.
  - The test call took place while it ran.
  - The keys in "See both legs as one call flow"
    showed what that section describes.
- Every test call carried audio both ways.
- On both, causing each fault under [When something does not
  work](#when-something-does-not-work) produced the message it quotes.

The examples use `192.0.2.10` as the machine's address. Replace it with yours
everywhere it appears.

## Install sipnab

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
V=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/NormB/sipnab/releases/latest \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["tag_name"].lstrip("v"))')
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb
curl -fsSL https://github.com/NormB/sipnab/releases/download/v$V/SHA256SUMS.txt \
  | grep " sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb$" | sha256sum -c -
sudo apt-get install -y ./sipnab_${V}_amd64.deb jq
sipnab --version
```

The commands in the sections from
"Explain the call from the saved capture"
to "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST"
use `jq` to pick fields out of sipnab's JSON. So the block installs it too.

## Watch a call through Asterisk

Start sipnab on every interface for 30 seconds.

- It prints each SIP message as it passes.
- It prints a report of the calls at the end.
- `-O` saves every packet it captured to `/tmp/asterisk-call.pcap`.
  - The sections "Explain the call from the saved capture"
    and "Ask about the call over MCP" use that
    file.

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -d any --duration 30 --report -O /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
```

While it runs, place a test call from a second terminal. Do it as in
[Place a test call in the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md#place-a-test-call):

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
cd ~/sipp
sipp -sf uas.xml -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5070 -min_rtp_port 7000 -max_rtp_port 7100 -rtp_echo -m 1 -bg
sudo sipp -sn uac_pcap 192.0.2.10:5060 -i 192.0.2.10 -p 5080 -s 100 -m 1 -timeout 90s
```

sipnab prints, in order:

- the caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
- then Asterisk's own `INVITE` to the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`.
  - It has a Call-ID Asterisk generated.
  - It has an SDP offer of its own.

When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the two legs as two calls. Both
are `Completed` with code `200`:

```text
Call-ID                          From           To             State        Code   Duration   Msgs   PDD      Tags
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1-50232@192.0.2.10               sipp           100            Completed    200    9s         7      0.0s     -
37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a...   sipp           -              Completed    200    9s         6      0.0s     -
```

- The first is the caller's leg, to extension `100`, with 7 messages.
  - Asterisk's `100 Trying` to the caller is among them.
- The second is Asterisk's leg to the callee, with 6.
  - Its `To` column shows `-`.
  - That is because Asterisk addressed the callee as `<sip:192.0.2.10>`, with
    no user name.

Below them, the `RTP Streams:` table shows that the audio goes through
Asterisk. Each leg has a different codec:

- On the caller's leg:
  - 236 `PCMA` packets from the caller to Asterisk,
  - 236 `PCMA` packets back, the callee's echo.
- On the callee's leg, 236 `PCMU` packets each way between Asterisk and the
  callee.
  - Asterisk converts the caller's PCMA to PCMU.
  - PCMU is the only codec the callee takes.
- The caller's key press: 10 `telephone-event` (DTMF) packets to Asterisk.
  - Asterisk passes it to the callee as a tone inside the audio.
  - So the callee's leg carries no `telephone-event` stream.
  - After the key press, both legs show short PCMU and PCMA streams under new
    SSRCs:
    - 6 `PCMU` packets each way on the callee's leg,
    - 10 `PCMA` packets toward the caller.

## See both legs as one call flow

The terminal interface shows the same calls, and updates as they happen:

```bash
sudo sipnab -d any
```

Place the test call from a second terminal, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk". The call list
shows two rows, one per leg. Both are `Completed`, with 7 and 6 messages. Then,
in the terminal interface:

- **Press `F4`** with the first row selected.
  - The extended flow draws both legs in one ladder with three columns:
    - the caller at `192.0.2.10:5080`,
    - Asterisk at `192.0.2.10:5060`,
    - the callee at `192.0.2.10:5070`.
  - The ladder shows these messages, in the order they happened:
    - the caller's `INVITE` to Asterisk,
    - Asterisk's `INVITE` to the callee,
    - the callee's answer,
    - Asterisk's answer to the caller.
  - Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Space`, `↓` (the down arrow), `Space` again, then `Enter`.**
  - `Space` stars the selected row, so this stars both legs.
  - With two rows starred, `Enter` opens one flow of both, in time order.
    It is the same three-column ladder.
  - Press `Esc` to go back to the list.
- **Press `Tab`** for the RTP streams.
  - Each stream names the leg it belongs to in the `Dialog` column.

Press `q`, then `y`, to quit.

## Explain the call from the saved capture

`--call-report` explains one call:

- its SIP transactions with their timings,
- for each audio stream, its packets, jitter, loss and estimated
  [MOS](@/docs/glossary.md#mos) (call quality on a scale from 1 to 5).

Reading a file needs no root. The first line finds the caller's leg in the
capture from "Watch a call through Asterisk":

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --json-dialogs --no-cli-print | jq -r 'select(.to == "100") | .call_id')
sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --call-report "$CALL" --no-cli-print
```

The report covers the caller's leg. Its `SIP Transactions` show:

- the `INVITE` answered in a few milliseconds,
- then the `ACK`,
- the `BYE` 9 seconds later:

```text
SIP Transactions:
  INVITE (SDP) -> 100 -> 180 (1ms) -> 200 (SDP) (3ms)
  ACK
  BYE -> 200 (9008ms)
```

Under `Media Streams`:

- The two PCMA streams of 236 packets, one each way, show no loss and
  `mos=4.36 R=90.8`.
- The `telephone-event` stream shows `mos=unknown (unpublished)`.
  - sipnab gives no quality estimate for DTMF events.
- The last stream is the 10 PCMA packets toward the caller.

The report ends with `Issues Detected: None`.

## Ask about the call over MCP

sipnab's MCP server lets an AI agent ask about a capture. The [MCP
guide](@/docs/mcp.md) sets it up for a client. This block does the following:

- It sends the three messages a client would, straight from the shell.
- It asks `find_correlated` which other leg belongs to the caller's call.
- Its first line takes the caller's Call-ID from the report. It uses the row
  whose `To` is `100`:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
CALL=$(sipnab -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --report --no-cli-print | awk '$3 == "100" {print $1}')
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"shell","version":"0"}}}' \
  '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' \
  "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":2,\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"find_correlated\",\"arguments\":{\"call_id\":\"$CALL\"}}}" \
  | sipnab --mcp -N -I /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap --quiet \
  | jq 'select(.id == 2) | .result.content[0].text | fromjson | {total_matched, heuristic_only, legs}'
```

The answer names Asterisk's leg:

```json
{
  "total_matched": 1,
  "heuristic_only": true,
  "legs": [
    {
      "call_id": "37e58306-c14d-4a0f-9fa1-41a2b3c05f96",
      "identifier_match": false,
      "observed_gap_ms": 1,
      "score": 50,
      "strategy": "timing_heuristic"
    }
  ]
}
```

`timing_heuristic` means that sipnab matched the legs for two reasons:

- They share an address.
- They started within 2 seconds of each other. Here they were 1 millisecond
  apart (`observed_gap_ms`).

That is a guess, and the answer says so:

- `identifier_match` is false.
- `heuristic_only` is true.

Asterisk puts no header on its leg that names the caller's leg. So sipnab has
no identifier to match on.

## Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST

The sipnab package installs a systemd service, `sipnab`. It captures on every
interface without the terminal interface. Turn on its REST API.

- sipnab reads the API key from the environment.
- Keep the key in a file only root can read. That keeps it out of the command
  line, where every user on the machine could read it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo sh -c 'umask 077; printf "SIPNAB_API_KEY=%s\n" "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" > /etc/sipnab/api.env'
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d/api.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/sipnab/api.env
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sipnab -N -d any --no-cli-print --syslog --metrics 127.0.0.1:9090 --api 127.0.0.1:8080
EOF
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sipnab
systemctl is-active sipnab
```

The `ExecStart` line keeps the package's own arguments and adds `--api`. The
API listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

Place the test call again, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk". Then ask
sipnab for:

- its calls,
- the leg that goes with the caller's,
- the audio streams:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
KEY=$(sudo sed -n 's/^SIPNAB_API_KEY=//p' /etc/sipnab/api.env)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs \
  | jq -r '.dialogs[] | [.call_id, .to_user // "-", .state, .msg_count] | @tsv'
CALL=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs | jq -r '.dialogs[] | select(.to_user == "100") | .call_id')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" "127.0.0.1:8080/v1/dialogs/$CALL/correlated" | jq -c '.legs[]'
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" 127.0.0.1:8080/v1/streams \
  | jq -r '.streams[] | [.associated_dialog, .codec, .packets, .loss_pct] | @tsv'
```

- The first answer lists the two legs, `Completed` with 7 and 6 messages.
- The second names Asterisk's leg with `"strategy":"timing_heuristic"`.
  - MCP did the same in "Ask about the call over MCP".
- The third lists each stream with:
  - the leg it belongs to,
  - its codec,
  - its packets,
  - its loss.

The [REST API reference](@/docs/api.md) gives every route.

## Receive Asterisk's HEP

[HEP](@/docs/glossary.md#hep) is the protocol SIP servers use to send a copy of their
traffic to a collector such as Homer.

- Asterisk sends HEP with its `res_hep` module.
  - The build in the Asterisk guide includes it.
- sipnab can receive it.
  - sipnab then sees the SIP as Asterisk handled it, with no capture on the
    wire.

Point Asterisk at sipnab's HEP listener, on port 9060 of the loopback address.
Then restart it:

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo tee /etc/asterisk/hep.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[general]
enabled = yes
capture_address = 127.0.0.1:9060
capture_id = 1234
uuid_type = call-id
EOF
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
until sudo asterisk -rx 'core waitfullybooted' 2>/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
sudo asterisk -rx 'module show like hep'
```

- The `until` line waits for Asterisk to finish starting. It works as in
  [Configure Asterisk in the Asterisk guide](@/docs/asterisk.md#configure-asterisk).
- `module show like hep` lists `res_hep.so`, `res_hep_pjsip.so` and
  `res_hep_rtcp.so` as `Running`.
- `capture_id` is the number Asterisk stamps on every copy it sends.
  - A collector uses it to tell its senders apart.
- `uuid_type
  = call-id` labels each copy with the SIP Call-ID.

Start sipnab's HEP listener for 30 seconds:

```bash
sudo sipnab -N -L 127.0.0.1:9060 --duration 30 --report --hep-senders
```

While it runs, place the test call from a second terminal, as in
"Watch a call through Asterisk".

- sipnab prints each message as it arrives, marked `origin=hep`.
- When the 30 seconds are up, the report lists the same two legs, and who sent
  them:

```text
  SOURCE                                PACKETS  LAST SEEN                    IDLE  STATE
  hep:1234@127.0.0.1                         15  2026-10-12T07:52:29.691Z      14s  sending
```

- `hep:1234` is Asterisk's `capture_id`.
- The last line counts `15 packets
  captured, 13 SIP messages`.
- The other two packets are RTCP summaries from `res_hep_rtcp`.
  - Asterisk sends them as JSON.
  - sipnab's report shows nothing from them.
- HEP carries no audio, so this report has no `RTP Streams:` table.
  - For the audio, capture on the wire as in
    "Watch a call through Asterisk".

HEP over UDP carries no authentication of its own. The capture id is what the
sender claims. Listening on `127.0.0.1` keeps every sender but this machine
out.

## Remove what this guide added

```bash
# Run all of these, in order.
sudo systemctl disable --now sipnab
sudo apt-get purge -y sipnab
sudo rm -rf /etc/systemd/system/sipnab.service.d /etc/sipnab
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo rm -f /etc/asterisk/hep.conf /tmp/asterisk-call.pcap
sudo systemctl restart asterisk
```

- `apt-get purge` removes the package and its own configuration.
- The API key file and the drop-in are yours, so the block removes them.
- The package leaves the `sipnab` user in place.

## When something does not work

- **sipnab says `sipnab: the terminal UI could not start: No such device or
  address (os error 6). It needs a terminal; add -N for a run without one.`**
  - The terminal interface needs an interactive terminal.
  - This session has none, as with a command passed to `ssh` without `-t`.
  - Run it from an interactive login, or use `-N` as in
    "Watch a call through Asterisk".
- **sipnab's HEP listener ends with `HEP listener on 127.0.0.1:9060 finished: 0
  packets received`.**
  - Asterisk sent nothing.
  - Run `sudo asterisk -rx 'module
    show like hep'`.
  - If the three modules show `Not Running`, Asterisk has not read
    `hep.conf`.
  - `core reload` does not start them. Restart Asterisk.
- **The REST API answers
  `{"status":401,"title":"Unauthorized","type":"https://sipnab.com/problems/unauthorized"}`.**
  - The request carried no API key, or the wrong one.
  - Read it from `/etc/sipnab/api.env`, as in
    "Keep sipnab running, and query it over REST".
